Vision–Language–Motion Maps: An Open-Vocabulary,
Uncertainty-Aware, Queryable Motion Attribute for 3D Scene Maps

Dibyendu Ghosh    Ayushi Shakya Affiliation: Rekise Marine, Bangalore, India Email: dibyendu35@gmail.com
Abstract

Open-vocabulary 3D maps let robots answer language queries about what and where, but they assume a static world and cannot answer queries about how scene elements behave. We introduce Vision–Language–Motion Maps (VLMM), an open-vocabulary, natural-language-queryable 3D map in which each element carries a fused motion attribute: a VLM/LLM semantic movability prior combined with geometrically observed cross-frame motion, together with a per-element uncertainty. Queries reduce to attribute filters that distinguish what has been seen to move, what could move but has not, and what stays still. On a controlled simulator benchmark with exact ground truth (AI2-THOR, three scene types) we show through ablation that the schema fields are non-substitutable: a semantic-only baseline fails motion queries even with strong features, and neither motion field substitutes for the other (the prior cannot answer “what is moving,” observed motion cannot answer “what could move”). On real dynamic RGB-D (TUM and Bonn, six sequences) we show the uncertainty channel—our key difference from prior fused-motion work— consistently improves moving-vs-static average precision and reduces false motion flags, and that it is robust to estimated (noisy) poses. The raw confidence is not calibrated, but post-hoc isotonic calibration reaches an expected calibration error of 0.100.10. VLMM is a representation contribution: the closest prior maps each lack at least one of the four properties—open-vocabulary, language-queryable, fused prior-and-observed motion, and per-element uncertainty—that our combination provides.

Index Terms—Semantic Scene Understanding, Mapping, RGB-D Perception, Deep Learning for Visual Perception.

I Introduction

A mobile robot that is told “the door that opens,” “things I could move,” or “where it stays still” needs more than a static semantic map: it must know how scene elements behave—a property existing maps largely do not represent, as we now survey.

Static open-vocabulary maps. VLMaps [1], ConceptFusion [2], ConceptGraphs [3], and HOV-SG [4] attach open-vocabulary visual–language features to top-down grids, voxels, or object nodes and answer natural-language spatial queries, but assume a static world and store no motion; VLMaps itself lists extending to “dynamic objects and moving humans” as future work.

“Dynamic” open-vocabulary maps as map maintenance. DynaMem [5] and DovSG [6] handle change by add/remove and re-perception, without a persistent, uncertainty-bearing, queryable motion field. DualMap [7]—closest to us—carries a CLIP anchor-vs-volatile movability prior and re-detects objects, but does not fuse the prior with measured geometric motion and stores no motion uncertainty.

Geometric and fused motion. Khronos [8] builds a 4D metric-semantic map from geometric motion detection but has no semantic prior, no stored per-element uncertainty, and no natural-language motion query. Dewan et al. [9] fuse a learned objectness prior with observed LiDAR motion in a Bayes filter (non-movable/movable/dynamic classes with a per-point belief), but are closed-set and not language-queryable. Voxeland [10] models per-instance semantic uncertainty but is static. Table I summarizes: no prior system provides all four of {open-vocabulary, language-queryable, fused prior×\timesobserved motion, per-element uncertainty}. We credit Dewan’s Bayesian belief and DualMap’s prior explicitly, so the distinction rests on the combination, not a single column.

We propose Vision–Language–Motion Maps (VLMM), whose map elements carry the schema

⟨\displaystyle\langle position,semantic_feat,observed_motion​(+conf),\displaystyle\text{position},\ \texttt{semantic\_feat},\ \texttt{observed\_motion}(\!+\!\text{conf}),
movability_prior,motion_class(+conf)⟩.\displaystyle\texttt{movability\_prior},\ \texttt{motion\_class}(\!+\!\text{conf})\,\rangle.

Our contributions are: (i) a queryable, uncertainty-aware fused motion attribute for open-vocabulary 3D maps; (ii) a geometric observed-motion channel that propagates range-dependent depth covariance into a Mahalanobis motion score, and that is robust to estimated poses via ego-motion refinement; (iii) a language-query interface that routes each query to a single schema field; and (iv) an evaluation that shows the schema fields are non-substitutable (no single field, including a strong semantic feature, answers the motion queries) across genuinely different scenes with exact ground truth, plus a characterization of where the contribution is strong (relative ablation, multi-scene uncertainty) and where it is not (absolute real-world accuracy, calibration).

II Method

VLMM represents a scene as a set of object-instance elements, each carrying a fused, uncertainty-aware motion attribute, and answers a natural-language query by routing it to a single schema field. Each element is built from two complementary channels: a semantic/appearance channel that yields an open-vocabulary feature and a movability prior, and a geometric channel that measures observed motion together with a propagated uncertainty. A confidence-aware rule fuses the two into a single motion_class, after which queries reduce to attribute filters over the schema (Fig. 1). We first fix notation, then describe the two channels, the fusion rule, and the query interface.

Notation. The map is a set of object-instance elements ℰ={ei}\mathcal{E}=\{e_{i}\}. Element ii is observed in keyframes through an instance mask ℳi⊂Ω\mathcal{M}_{i}\!\subset\!\Omega (pixel domain Ω\Omega) and stores

ei=(𝐩i,𝐟i,oi,κi,ρi,yi,ci),e_{i}=\big(\mathbf{p}_{i},\ \mathbf{f}_{i},\ o_{i},\ \kappa_{i},\ \rho_{i},\ y_{i},\ c_{i}\big),

position 𝐩i∈ℝ3\mathbf{p}_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{3}, semantic feature 𝐟i\mathbf{f}_{i}, observed-motion score oi≥0o_{i}\!\geq\!0 with reliability κi∈[0,1]\kappa_{i}\!\in\![0,1], movability prior ρi∈[0,1]\rho_{i}\!\in\![0,1], fused class yi∈𝒴={static,movable_static,moving}y_{i}\!\in\!\mathcal{Y}\!=\!\{\textsc{static},\textsc{movable\_static},\textsc{moving}\}, and class confidence cic_{i}. Camera intrinsics are KK; the pose of keyframe tt is Tt=(Rt,𝐭t)∈S​E​(3)T_{t}=(R_{t},\mathbf{t}_{t})\in SE(3) (camera-to-world), known or estimated. Fig. 2 shows the resulting map on real keyframes across three scenes: each object instance carries the schema, and a natural-language query highlights the instances matching a single field.

II-A Semantic channel

The semantic feature is an open-vocabulary region-CLIP embedding: the full CLIP image encoder [11, 12] is applied to the instance’s masked crop,

𝐟i=CLIPimg(crop(I,ℳi))/∥⋅∥2,\mathbf{f}_{i}=\mathrm{CLIP}_{\mathrm{img}}\!\big(\mathrm{crop}(I,\mathcal{M}_{i})\big)\big/\big\|\!\cdot\!\big\|_{2}, (1)

which is markedly more discriminative than dense MaskCLIP [13] features and gives a strong semantic-only baseline (the ConceptFusion/ConceptGraphs paradigm). A language query qq scores element ii by cosine similarity si​(q)=𝐟i⊤​CLIPtxt​(q)s_{i}(q)=\mathbf{f}_{i}^{\!\top}\,\mathrm{CLIP}_{\mathrm{txt}}(q).

Dense optical flow [14] gives the correspondence u′=u+𝐰a→b​(u)u^{\prime}=u+\mathbf{w}_{a\to b}(u) in keyframe bb, with a forward–backward consistency mask 𝒱\mathcal{V} (we keep uu iff ∥𝐰a→b​(u)+𝐰b→a​(u′)∥<ϵ\lVert\mathbf{w}_{a\to b}(u)+\mathbf{w}_{b\to a}(u^{\prime})\rVert<\epsilon and depth is valid at both ends). Σc\displaystyle\Sigma^{c} =J​diag​(σpx2,σpx2,σz2​(z))​J⊤,\displaystyle=J\,\mathrm{diag}\!\big(\sigma_{\mathrm{px}}^{2},\sigma_{\mathrm{px}}^{2},\sigma_{z}^{2}(z)\big)\,J^{\!\top}, (6)

which, unlike a fixed diagonal model, correctly couples depth error into the lateral world axes for off-centre pixels. Motion is scored by the Mahalanobis magnitude (Fig. 3b)

dM​(u)=𝐦~​(u)⊤​Σm−1​𝐦~​(u).d_{M}(u)=\sqrt{\tilde{\mathbf{m}}(u)^{\!\top}\,\Sigma_{m}^{-1}\,\tilde{\mathbf{m}}(u)}. (7)

Decision as a hypothesis test. Under the null (static) hypothesis H0:𝔼⁡[𝐦~]=𝟎H_{0}\!:\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{m}}]=\mathbf{0}, the residual is zero-mean Gaussian, so dM2∼χ32d_{M}^{2}\sim\chi^{2}_{3} and the gate dM>τd_{M}>\tau is a per-point likelihood-ratio test whose threshold τ=χ3, 1−α2\tau=\sqrt{\chi^{2}_{3,\,1-\alpha}} is fixed by a single static false-flag level α\alpha (e.g. α=0.05⇒τ≈2.80\alpha\!=\!0.05\Rightarrow\tau\!\approx\!2.80). The tail probability pmot​(u)=Pr⁡(χ32>dM2)p_{\mathrm{mot}}(u)=\Pr\!\big(\chi^{2}_{3}>d_{M}^{2}\big) is the static-consistency pp-value. Hence far/noisy points inflate Σm\Sigma_{m}, shrink dMd_{M}, and are not false-flagged—the threshold adapts to range instead of being a fixed metric distance.

Per-object aggregation. Over valid instance pixels 𝒫i=ℳi∩𝒱\mathcal{P}_{i}=\mathcal{M}_{i}\cap\mathcal{V}, the object score is the 7575th percentile of dMd_{M} and the reliability is the product of a fraction-moving term ϕi\phi_{i} and a coherence term γi\gamma_{i}:

oi=Q75​{dM​(u):u∈𝒫i},κi=ϕi​γi,o_{i}=\mathrm{Q}_{75}\{d_{M}(u):u\in\mathcal{P}_{i}\},\qquad\kappa_{i}=\phi_{i}\,\gamma_{i}, (8)
ϕi\displaystyle\phi_{i} =1|𝒫i|∑u∈𝒫i[dM(u)>τ],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{i}|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{P}_{i}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[d_{M}(u)>\tau\right], (9)
γi\displaystyle\gamma_{i} =∥1|𝒫i|​∑u∈𝒫i𝐦~​(u)∥𝐦~​(u)∥∥,\displaystyle=\Bigg\lVert\,\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{i}|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{P}_{i}}\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{m}}(u)}{\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{m}}(u)\rVert}\,\Bigg\rVert, (10)

i.e. ϕi\phi_{i} is the fraction of pixels above the motion-noise floor and γi\gamma_{i} the directional coherence (mean resultant length) of the residual vectors. Hence κi\kappa_{i} is high only when a coherent fraction of the instance moves together (a rigid mover), and low for boundary/flow bleed.

II-C Movability prior

ρi=VLM⁡(ℓi)∈[0,1]\rho_{i}=\mathrm{VLM}(\ell_{i})\in[0,1] answers “can a ℓi\ell_{i} move?” for the object’s open-vocabulary label ℓi\ell_{i}, queried once per category and cached (no per-frame VLM cost).

II-D Fusion rule

A confidence-aware rule maps the two channels to the class yiy_{i}; high-confidence observed motion overrides the prior, while unreliable/absent motion defers to it:

yi={movingif ​oi>τo∧κi≥κo,movable_staticelse if ​ρi≥ρτ,staticotherwise.y_{i}=\begin{cases}\textsc{moving}&\text{if }o_{i}>\tau_{o}\,\wedge\,\kappa_{i}\geq\kappa_{o},\\[2.0pt] \textsc{movable\_static}&\text{else if }\rho_{i}\geq\rho_{\tau},\\[2.0pt] \textsc{static}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (11)

with class confidence ci=κic_{i}=\kappa_{i} for moving and ci=ρic_{i}=\rho_{i} (resp. 1−ρi1-\rho_{i}) for movable_static (resp. static). The thresholds (τo,κo,ρτ)(\tau_{o},\kappa_{o},\rho_{\tau}) make the rule a small, swappable function.

II-E Query interface

A natural-language query is parsed to a structured filter ⟨s,𝑓𝑖𝑒𝑙𝑑,𝑟𝑒𝑡⟩\langle s,\ \mathit{field},\ \mathit{ret}\rangle: an optional semantic text ss, a return type 𝑟𝑒𝑡\mathit{ret} (object or mask), and a single target field that is one of observed_motion, movability_prior, motion_class, or none. The executor returns

{ei:si​(s)≥θs∧π𝑓𝑖𝑒𝑙𝑑​(ei)},\{\,e_{i}:s_{i}(s)\geq\theta_{s}\ \wedge\ \pi_{\mathit{field}}(e_{i})\,\}, (12)

where π\pi is the field predicate (e.g. yi=movingy_{i}\!=\!\textsc{moving} for “the door that opens”, ρi≥ρτ\rho_{i}\!\geq\!\rho_{\tau} for “things I could move”, yi=staticy_{i}\!=\!\textsc{static} returning a mask for “where it stays still”). Each intent thus touches exactly one field. We use a rule-based parser and report its generalization in Sec. III. An LLM front-end would emit the same ⟨s,𝑓𝑖𝑒𝑙𝑑,𝑟𝑒𝑡⟩\langle s,\mathit{field},\mathit{ret}\rangle filter; since we have not evaluated one, we mark NL querying partial for VLMM in Table I (the motion attribute is language-queryable; the current parser is rule-based).

Because motion and movability are object-level properties, VLMM stores per-object elements rather than a per-voxel feature volume; a query is therefore an attribute filter over the element set (Eq. 12), not a nearest-neighbour lookup over a feature grid as in voxel-based open-vocabulary maps. Fig. 2 visualizes the resulting per-object attributes projected onto real keyframes; for grid-based planners they can additionally be rasterized into an occupancy grid on demand.

III Results & Discussion

III-A Implementation and compute

The full system is implemented in Python 3.10 with PyTorch 2.5. The semantic channel uses open_clip ViT-B/16 [12]; the observed-motion channel uses RAFT optical flow [14]; a YOLOv8-seg model supplies instance masks on real RGB-D; and the embodied study runs in the AI2-THOR [16] simulator. All experiments run on a single laptop-class GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4060, 8 GB)—an explicit design constraint. To stay within 8 GB we (i) cache per-keyframe dense CLIP features to disk so peak VRAM never holds all frames at once, (ii) treat the VLM/LLM movability prior as a cached per-category call (no per-frame cost), and (iii) avoid any component that needs a multi-GPU server.

III-B Datasets

Simulator (exact ground truth). AI2-THOR provides, per object, an instance mask, movability flags (pickupable/moveable), and exact motion (objects are displaced by known deltas). We render three genuinely different scene types—kitchen, living room, bedroom (67 observed objects)—and use them for the field-necessity ablation because every label is exact; camera geometry was validated to 1.11.1 cm cross-view static-point alignment. Real RGB-D. TUM RGB-D [17] (walking_static, walking_xyz, walking_rpy, desk_with_person) and the Bonn dynamic dataset [18] (crowd, person_tracking) give six real noisy dynamic sequences across two labs/sensors; moving-region ground truth comes from a person segmenter (a proxy; see Limitations). Note the AI2-THOR scenes contain no people—every mover is a household object (Kettle, Pan, Book, Laptop, Bowl, Tissue Box)—so the motivating non-person “door that opens” query is evaluated directly with exact, non-proxy ground truth (Q_moving, Table II); the person proxy is only the real-data stand-in.

III-C Evaluation metrics and parameters

We report average precision (AP) and precision/recall/F1 for moving-vs-static detection and for the attribute queries—not accuracy, since true negatives dominate—mask IoU for region queries, and expected calibration error (ECE) [19] for confidence. Key settings, fixed across all scenes: region-CLIP crops at 640640 px; RAFT with a 22 px forward–backward consistency gate; the depth-noise model [15] (a,b,z0)=(1.2,1.9,0.4)×10−3(a,b,z_{0})\!=\!(1.2,1.9,0.4)\!\times\!10^{-3} with lateral σpx=1.5\sigma_{\mathrm{px}}\!=\!1.5; ego-refinement by RANSAC (22 cm inlier threshold) and Kabsch; per-object score oi=Q75​(dM)o_{i}=\mathrm{Q}_{75}(d_{M}); frame gap kk chosen per dataset; and a single fixed fusion threshold triple (τo,κo,ρτ)(\tau_{o},\kappa_{o},\rho_{\tau}). Every reported number traces to one pinned run per experiment.

Threshold sensitivity. The reported AP and false-flag numbers are rank-based and therefore independent of the fusion thresholds; only the discrete motion_class assignment depends on (τo,κo,ρτ)(\tau_{o},\kappa_{o},\rho_{\tau}). On the exact-GT maps (67 objects) observed motion cleanly separates movers (dM∈[0.69,3.65]d_{M}\!\in\![0.69,3.65]) from non-movers (dM≤0.05d_{M}\!\leq\!0.05), so the motion gate is insensitive across an order of magnitude τo∈[0.05,0.69]\tau_{o}\!\in\![0.05,0.69] (3-class macro-F1 constant at 0.9050.905), degrading only once τo\tau_{o} exceeds the slowest mover’s score. The movability gate is more sensitive: macro-F1 ∈[0.905,0.966]\in[0.905,0.966] over ρτ∈[0.40,0.60]\rho_{\tau}\!\in\![0.40,0.60] and falls to 0.770.77 by ρτ=0.70\rho_{\tau}\!=\!0.70; our fixed ρτ=0.55\rho_{\tau}\!=\!0.55 is conservative, not tuned (lower values score higher). We thus place τo\tau_{o} in the wide observed-motion gap and report the ρτ\rho_{\tau} dependence openly.

III-D Schema fields are non-substitutable (exact-GT ablation)

Table II reports AP on three THOR scenes. We read it as a non-substitutability check, not a discovery of necessity: since a query routes to a single field, the diagonal (a query losing its own field) is partly definitional. The informative content is therefore (a) whether strong semantics alone can answer the motion queries, and (b) the off-diagonal—whether one motion field can substitute for the other. Both are negative. Semantic-only fails the motion query (0.100.10, near the 0.090.09 random rate) even with strong region-CLIP features: image semantics do not encode observed motion, so the failure is fundamental, not a weak-feature artifact. The two motion channels are not interchangeable: the prior alone scores only 0.300.30 on “what is moving” (movability ≠\neq observed motion), while observed-motion alone collapses “what could move” and “stays still” (an unmoved movable object reveals no motion). Only the full schema answers all three. The uncertainty weighting ties here on exact depth (rows iv and v) and separates only under sensor noise (Table III)—it is a real-noise property, not a clean-sim one. Fig. 4 makes this concrete: on “what is moving” the semantic-only baseline returns the wrong instances while VLMM, ranking by observed_motion, returns exactly the ground-truth movers.

Measured baselines. The two dominant prior designs, reimplemented on the same exact-GT data, both fail the motion query. A VLMaps/ConceptFusion-style CLIP map (per-element features by text similarity), queried with the best of six phrasings (incl. “the door that opens”), reaches only AP =0.18=0.18 on “what is moving” (random 0.090.09) versus VLMM’s 1.001.00— appearance features do not encode instantaneous motion—though it partially answers “what could move” (0.660.66), since movability is semantic. DualMap’s anchor-vs-volatile mechanism (CLIP similarity to a static-category template) answers “what could move” well (0.800.80) but conflates moving with movable: only 0.320.32 on “what is moving,” as an anchor/volatile state cannot isolate the currently-moving subset. Both lack the observed-motion channel VLMM adds; these are the documented mechanisms, not the released systems (Limitations).

III-E Uncertainty is the differentiator (multi-scene)

The uncertainty channel separates VLMM from Dewan’17. Table III shows that switching the raw world-displacement score to the Mahalanobis score improves moving-vs-static AP in all six real sequences (mean +0.10+0.10) and reduces the far-static false-flag rate in all six. On exact-GT sim, the two are tied on noise-free depth (nothing to be uncertain about) but diverge by +0.27+0.27 AP once we inject a Kinect-quadratic depth noise σ=0.0012+0.0028​z2\sigma=0.0012+0.0028\,z^{2} (Table III, last rows). We stress that this injected noise is deliberately different from the method’s assumed covariance (the Nguyen axial model of Sec. III-C): the method only approximates the true sensor noise, so the test is fair rather than self-confirming: uncertainty is neutral on clean depth and essential under real sensor noise.

III-F Calibration

The raw per-element motion confidence is not calibrated: ECE =0.30=0.30 (pooled, 4.8M pixels), overconfident. It is rank-useful (it drives the +0.10+0.10 AP). A standard post-hoc isotonic calibration, fit on TUM and tested held-out on Bonn, reaches ECE =0.10=0.10 (Fig. 5a,b). We therefore claim “uncertainty-weighted, post-hoc calibratable,” not “well-calibrated.”

III-G Robustness to estimated poses

The observed-motion channel assumes known poses. Fig. 5c,d injects per-frame pose error: with ego-refinement the AP is invariant to pose error (it re-derives the relative pose from static structure), while without it AP degrades (Bonn →0.220.32\!\rightarrow\!0.22 at 1.5∘/31.5^{\circ}/3 cm). The channel therefore does not require accurate SLAM poses (assuming a dominantly-static scene).

III-H Query interface and parser

The three canonical queries plus paraphrases route to the correct field; a confidence threshold on “reliably static” trades recall for precision (→1.000.81\!\rightarrow\!1.00). On 30 held-out paraphrases the rule parser routes 24/30=80%24/30=80\% correctly, failing on negation—confirming it is intent routing, not language understanding (an LLM parser is the camera-ready fix).

IV Limitations

(1) The strong ablation numbers are exact-GT simulation; real-world object-level F1 is ≈0.5\approx 0.5 (motion-bleed; flow under-measures small/fast objects)—we claim relative, not SOTA, results. (2) Confidence is uncertainty-weighted, not raw-calibrated. (3) The query parser is intent routing, not NLU. (4) Real-data motion GT is a person segmenter, conflating “moving” with “person” (static people are false positives, non-person movers missed); the real-data numbers (Table III) thus establish the uncertainty channel’s effect under sensor noise, not general non-person detection—which we evaluate only in simulation (exact GT, incl. injected Kinect-level noise, +0.27+0.27 gap). A real non-person-mover benchmark is the main remaining gap. (5) We measure VLMaps- and DualMap-style baselines (documented mechanisms, shared data; Sec. III); the full released systems remain. (6) Motion thresholds need per-sensor calibration; the ranking is the scale-robust quantity.

V Conclusion

VLMM adds a queryable, uncertainty-aware, fused motion attribute to open-vocabulary 3D maps. The combination is novel against the closest prior art; the schema fields are shown non-substitutable on exact-GT multi-scene simulation; and the uncertainty channel—the differentiator from prior fused-motion work—is validated across six real noisy sequences and under realistic sensor noise in simulation. Calibration and the scope of the claims are reported in full, leaving a real non-person-mover benchmark and a released-baseline comparison as future work.
